sentences.text: Because brands and retailers just don't really have any software to help them truly understand what the effect of investment is achieving.

So we've got lots of data scientists that have done a really good job of over 10,000 insight reports that actually genuinely disclose how effective combinations of media are and what likely return on investment they would get.
And that's helping people plan with precision, get better return on investment.
And what we've realized is that even though our heritage was working directly with retailers and lots of brands, I'm very proud.
Actually.
In the last two years we've opened up offices, one in Sydney and one also in Uruguay and Latin America.
And we're finding that those regions are very, very, very bullish in terms of their approach to the future of retail media.
In fact, we're very proud.
Again, we've got a grant from the Uruguayan government to help kind of evolve retail media in the Latam region, which is going very well.
And we've had various envoy trips backwards and forwards to, to get that off the ground.
So, yeah, that's a long introduction.
Sorry, Zach.
No, no, no, it's great, it's great to hear what you guys are doing, Stuart.
So, yeah, just a couple, a couple questions for you.
How many can you give me just a high level on like how many customers you guys work with roughly?
And is the majority of the business kind of concentrated in a customers or is it kind of spread out pretty evenly?
I think broadly it's spread out pretty evenly.
So we've got three separate arms to the business.
We've got our core tech business, which is we call base, and we've got two, I suppose, service arms.
One is called rmi, which looks after retailers who need some support, and one is called smi, that looks after brand owners that need some support.
So, and if I said sort of broadly, our tech is used by people like Sainsbury's, Iceland, W.H.
smith, SSP.
It's been used in the past by people like Co Op, bp.
It's, it's, it's people of that built and scale we're currently providing insight services, have done for like seven or eight years now for Heineken.
They, they joined us at a point where they were getting around about $2 ROI for every dollar invested.
That was about seven or eight years ago.
It's now up to about $12 for every dollar invested through our help and support, which is pretty magnificent actually.
They're delighted.
It's sort of set their playbook for their entire global investment strategy into retail media.
But we also do that for Fox's Burtons, we do it for Bird's Eye.
And what's great about that is that those companies, once we've got them in one territory, they tend to expand.
So we just signed up Belgium as an example with Heineken.
They've also looked over the shoulder, look what the UK are up to and gone.
We want some of that as well.
When it comes to retailers like ssp, they're actually travel retailers.
They do airside, they do train stations and airports and I mean, they have thousands of outlets catering, but they have digital screens and point of sale, all that kind of stuff.
They're operating in 32 markets all over the world.
And we've hit the ground running in the uk, but they're in the process now of exploring how they can expand that out into APAC and other places.

If you think about what we do with working with retailers, we've got access to upwards of 6 or 700 different brand owners that we work with regularly over the year, and we offer them some form of creative services.

So if there is a need to create a banner ad or some digital screen activity or some printed point of sale, a kind of byproduct that we can add on and say, if, you know, you want us to help you get that done, we can design that for you.
So it stems out from the tech.
Very cool.
And so, Stuart, what makes you guys want to, if you don't mind me asking, like, look for an exit now in the business?
What's.
What?
How would you think about the timing?
Or is there something around that?
That's a great question.
I'm 54 and I'm loving what I'm doing right now.
I've got to be honest, Zach, when Covid hit, my business partner was diagnosed with prostate cancer.
He's absolutely fine.
He's got through it, he's in remission, but he stepped away from the business, well, five years ago, and he's now through his treatment and would really like to just get on with the rest of his life.
So that was the, I suppose, the impetus for us to approach Andy because, you know, ultimately John would like to be able to sort of enjoy some time with his family and kids and what have you.
He's slightly older than me, he's just coming up to 60.
Um, but for me, it's all about scale now.
You know, I've put.
Put the years into.
To get it to a point where I'm so excited about actually seeing this transcend into a truly global business.
And I'VE got to say that the growth that I've seen the cool company achieve from, you know, a little bit of Googling and web research that I've done is, is just phenomenal.
I don't know how you've managed to achieve that, Zach, but as I said to you at the start, hats off.
Amazing.
Thank you.
I appreciate it.
It's been a very interesting journey as, as yours has definitely been as well.
And so Stuart, do you want to.
And thank you for that.
And it's really impressive what you guys have built.
Really impressive.
Thank you.
Is it a good assumption that like you, you, you'd like to stay on to help kind of.
Would you be interested in staying on to help kind of grow in this next evolution with, with whoever the, the buyer is?
Is that something you're interested in or 100%.
Okay.
And our management team as well actually Zach, you know, we're very close that we've got option scheme.
So basically they've got a, a bit of the action and incentivized to stay and be part of that, that growth phase that we see ourselves entering into.
Yeah.
Simple answer to a simple question.
Okay.
All right.
Very, very cool.
What would you say?
It seems like you guys have a lot of really exciting growth levers that are happening right now is have you guys done anything in the US market?
Is that something that you've talked about or thought about or something you kind of have said hey no, we're going to focus to really own these other markets.
How have you thought about that?
Yeah, we've, I suppose the term is we've kissed a lot of frogs over the last sort of 10 years.
We had a strategic partnership with Dentsu Aegis that was probably, that was pre covered.

We had an office in their New York office office just opposite Grand Central Station and I spent a lot of time over there and we met with key clients like Walmart, Home Depot, Coca Cola, Beiersdorf and there was.
It was clear to me then that the sort of the ascension of retail media was, was going to be absolutely enormous at that point in time.
Americ a few steps behind where Europe was.
I think there's a degree of catch up that's happened.
I think I've witnessed also.
I mean there used to be things like News America and almost a syndicated approach to install retail media.
They kind of sold it off and let other people worry about what was going to be erected and put up in front of the customer.

But they've all reclaimed control over that now and they're in the process of building out the equivalence of their kind of Dun Humbees, Nectar360 particularly is it 8171, the Kroger outfit and other people like that.
So I understand the American market and in fact I've had a million dollar contract with png.

But the irony of the whole things act was when I was talking and liaising with large agency groups, they were very scared about retail media because it wasn't fluffy, it wasn't idealistic, they didn't know how to charge for it and they didn't like the level of detail that was involved.
They were very much more high level.

Now, the world's moved on clearly a long way since then, but I think to this day the only kind of large agency groups that really got it are people like publicists who have acquired a number of players in my space and I think, you know, largely people like Dentsu, wpp, Omnicom, they're all going to find themselves in a whole heap of trouble because they're just not close enough to understanding this.
So it's a long way of answering a question which is I think the American market is absolutely brilliant, well primed for what we have.

I've met with retailers over there like Maya, so I'm aware of kind of like the regional players of which there are dozens, probably hundreds across the states that all have a need for a very complex operating system which we have out the box.
And I think that's pretty where, you know, we are in the process of building out with Sainsbury's and Accenture, their unified platform, which is.
We're under NDA and this isn't public knowledge yet, but base our software system is at the very heart and the core of what they do.
And there's over a third of a billion pounds that goes through that each year and we do all of the billing for them.
So we've got every educator covered.
You know, we can operate for someone of the skies of size of Saints plc.
We can operate for any retailer on the planet, genuinely.
So we know that people like them and Walmart, Albert Hein, who's part of our whole.

Dal Hayes, you know, you have a handful of large retailers who are prepared to spend upwards of 15 to 20 million dollars to build an operating system that can help them scale their retail media outfit.

Where do you see the market headed, Stuart?
Like what do you think?
Aside from obviously growth and penetration, where do you see the market headed over the next two to three years?
So by market I would, I would turn that retail media, I think from a digital proposition perspective, you know, everybody understands supply side, demand side.
It's all about on site, off site.
You can analyze that through AI, through.
It's absolutely saturated with incredibly powerful software packages.
And you know, clearly retailers understand the power of their online proposition and the value of their audience and the ability to target through loyalty based information, all that kind of stuff.
I think the sort of consumer market, direct consumer for brand owners is going to be quite significant.

I think CPG is going to try and take back quite a lot of control in terms of the relationship with the customer and not necessarily rely on the retailer themselves having all of the aces up their sleeve.
But that aside, I think, you know, the, the slow but sure digitization of stores is going to continue.
I mean I live in London, you live in a metropolis and you know, you can clearly walk up and down the road and see a lot of investment going into digital signage, digital ends, that kind of thing.
But you know, you walk into the middle of Delaware or you know, slightly more tertiary outfits.
It does not make sense to have everything digitized all at once.
So there is still a massive, massive void that needs filling for retailers globally.
I mean I spent a lot of time in Indonesia actually talking to retailers over there and enormous country, upwards of 350 million people.
But it's spread out so you can't have distribution networks and you can't have to, so you can't do things like next day delivery or those kind of things.
It's all about people into the store.
So I think it's about normalization and that's where I think we will play a huge role which is allowing retailers and brands to have almost like a trade desk of omnichannel retail media.

And that's what I've set out to achieve, which is build a platform which is community driven across every market, in every currency that allows people to contribute their touch points, SKUs, rate cards, specification sheets and act as a central kind of fulcrum of a wheel to distribute content from so that people can go through the workflow which again is quite complex when you think about all the moving parts to get something on site, off site, in store, published, printed, distributed proof of concept, proof of execution, subsequent evaluation.

It's about holistically holding all that data in the same place in a normalized way that allows for an even playing field to develop for retailers and CPGs globally to trade the true value of what their, their media is.
And actually the true value of their media is far greater than that of TV or press or traditional verticals that have dominated for the last 80 years.
So there's no doubt in my mind that retailers will continue to become the, the dominant media owner globally.

summary.overview: In the Sales/Acquisition Discussion meeting between Cool Company and TSG, Stuart presented an overview of TSG's capabilities, highlighting its role in helping brands and retailers measure media investment effectiveness, with a strong portfolio of clients including Sainsbury's and Heineken. He discussed TSG’s current business structure, including its three arms and recent expansion into Latin America, as well as his partner’s intent to exit following health recovery. The conversation then delved into TSG’s software, which supports rapid implementation for retailers and aims to create a unified omnichannel platform, positioning retailers as future media owners. Stuart expressed a desire for the transaction structure to reflect potential growth, while also ensuring the management team is incentivized to stay. Next steps include sharing a demo video and opening a data room for financial review, with Cool Company poised as a suitable acquirer given its experience with Carrefour. Action items were assigned to Andy for follow-up tasks.
